title: Ethics of boosting performance

draft.title: Ethics of boosting performance
card: Fairness
Sport is meant to be a contest on equal terms. An athlete using banned substances or methods gains an advantage that clean competitors do not have.
Health
Banned substances and methods can harm the body, sometimes for life. Athletes may risk their long-term health for short-term success.
Spirit of sport
Sport values honesty, effort and respect for the rules. Cheating goes against these values and can damage trust in sport.
Pressure
Athletes may feel pressure from coaches, sponsors, fans or rivals to win. This pressure can push some towards banned methods.
draft.remember: Boosting with banned means raises issues of fairness, health, the spirit of sport and pressure.

a.q: A swimmer uses a banned substance and beats clean rivals. Which ethical issue does this mainly raise?
opts: Fairness, as rivals compete without the advantage
Health, as the win proves the swimmer is fit
Pressure, as clean rivals feel forced to cheat
Spirit of sport, as honesty is made stronger
a.why: Clean rivals compete without the advantage, so the contest is not on equal terms. The win does not show fitness, and cheating works against the spirit of sport rather than strengthening it.
a.clue: Think about whether everyone started on equal terms.

b.q: A young runner in Bendigo is told by a sponsor that her funding will end if she stops winning. She considers a banned drug. Which issue does this best show?
opts: Pressure on athletes to win
The spirit of sport being upheld
Fairness being improved for rivals
Health being protected by the drug
b.why: The threat to funding is pressure from outside that can push an athlete towards banned methods. The other options are the opposite of what banned drugs do: they harm the spirit of sport, fairness and health.
b.clue: Who is pushing her, and why?

a.best: Fairness, as rivals compete without the advantage

problems.detail: All three distractors are plainly false on their face (a banned drug 'protecting' health, 'improving' fairness, 'upholding' the spirit of sport), so a Year 11 student can get this right by elimination without understanding the ideas.

check.summary: The card, remember line and both questions are accurate and match the explanations. The only issue is that question b's wrong options are so implausible that the question is too easy for Year 11.

flags: Question b, level: All three distractors are plainly false on their face (a banned drug 'protecting' health, 'improving' fairness, 'upholding' the spirit of sport), so a Year 11 student can get this right by elimination without understanding the ideas.

proposal.title: Ethics of boosting performance
card: Fairness
Sport is meant to be a contest on equal terms. An athlete using banned substances or methods gains an advantage that clean competitors do not have.
Health
Banned substances and methods can harm the body, sometimes for life. Athletes may risk their long-term health for short-term success.
Spirit of sport
Sport values honesty, effort and respect for the rules. Cheating goes against these values and can damage trust in sport.
Pressure
Athletes may feel pressure from coaches, sponsors, fans or rivals to win. This pressure can push some towards banned methods.
proposal.remember: Boosting with banned means raises issues of fairness, health, the spirit of sport and pressure.

a.q: A weightlifter knows a banned drug may damage his heart in later life. He takes it to win this season. Which issue does accepting that risk show?
opts: Health, trading long-term harm for a short-term win
Fairness, gaining an edge that clean rivals lack
Pressure, being pushed by others to keep winning
Spirit of sport, breaking the value of honesty
a.why: Accepting possible heart damage later for a win now is the health issue. Fairness is also raised by doping, but the question asks about the risk to his own body, not his rivals.
a.clue: What is he putting at risk, and for how long?

b.q: A young runner in Bendigo is told by a sponsor that her funding will end if she stops winning. She has not taken any drug yet. Which issue does the sponsor's threat show?
opts: Pressure from others to keep winning
Fairness between her and clean rivals
Harm to her long-term health
Loss of trust in honest sport
b.why: The sponsor is pushing her to win by threatening her funding, which is pressure that can lead athletes towards banned methods. Fairness, health and trust would come into play only if she used a banned drug, and she has not.
b.clue: Focus on the threat itself, not on a drug she has not taken.
